A failed-attempt status order must have at least one failed attempt, so 643 orders cannot coexist with 424 attempts; this undermines the attempt/order distinction the analysis emphasizes.

The fixed 'Prototype controls' panel (styles.css L691-L692) overlays the data: it covers the 5-6 Nov bars and part of the rate chart in screenshots/desktop.png and the on-time KPI card in screenshots/mobile.png.

strengths: The headline answers what changed immediately: 85.0%, down 1.3 pp, West -4.9 pp, 712 late deliveries.
Freshness is rigorous: data through 7 Nov 14:05, last complete day 6 Nov, exact period and comparison dates, with the 15-minute lag stated without alarm.
Deep, context-preserving investigation: chart-day drill, an orders view with period/region/status/day chips, and an order drawer with focus trap and focus return.
Clear visualization discipline: separate small multiples, zero baselines, a sorted-lowest region table, pp versus percent, and status chips with icon, text and pattern.
States beyond the basic set: an undefined rate for non-delivered status, an empty drill-down distinct from period-level no-data, and partial coverage with unreported regions disabled.

comparison: Candidate A is the stronger metric-definition and transparency artifact: its definitions, denominators, units and state model are internally consistent, and the numbers reconcile across KPIs, regions and statuses. Candidate B has the cleaner responsive composition and the deeper interaction model (chart-day drill, custom range, order drawer), and its headline is faster to scan, but its status mix contradicts its failed-attempt KPI (643 failed-status orders versus 424 attempts) and its fixed prototype panel hides chart data in both screenshots. Visual hierarchy is comparable: Candidate A has a stronger focal KPI but a nearly flat 0-100% rate chart, while Candidate B is cleaner but flattens the three KPIs and overlays content. Weighted scores (15/20/15/15/15/10/10): Candidate A 3.40, Candidate B 3.50.
limitations: One blinded judge pass, not a statistical test. Both packets supply a 1280px desktop screenshot, a roughly 390px mobile capture, the full implementation and one rendered-checks file, so the visual-hierarchy comparison is scoreable; Candidate A's mobile image is 580px wide because of its document overflow. Only the ready state is captured for either candidate: stale, partial, no-data, error, empty and undefined states are evidenced only by code and prose. Neither packet contains the output of Candidate A's claimed 39 DOM checks or Candidate B's claimed structural checks, nor a screen-reader or manual WCAG session; the accessibility scores rely on the axe summaries in checks.json, which are not proof of conformance. I did not execute either prototype, so state transitions, keyboard behavior and the source of Candidate A's mobile overflow are inferred from code and captured checks. Candidate A's analysis says no axe engine was run and 375px was not inspected, which conflicts with checks.json (axe results and a 390px mobile capture); the machine output was treated as authoritative. No mapping or material outside the pass inputs was read.
